scientific_queries.note: Same-class audit of C42, applying the lesson written in R95.

subagent_note: None dispatched: the round hunts for a flaw of the kind found twice in a row, does not find one, and says so plainly.
audit_target: C42: 'decision value of a weak signal is insensitive to pool size (with a proportional budget)' - the parenthetical was the tell

design.manipulation: pool size only, via uniform subsampling of keys from 2,000 to 20,000, so composition is held fixed
design.predictor: drug marginals computed once on the full pool so that only the evaluation pool varies

audit_outcome.hypothesis: C42's insensitivity might be produced by its proportional-budget rule
audit_outcome.result: not confirmed - the fixed-budget rule is also flat, so insensitivity is not a budget-rule artefact

why_it_is_flat_regardless_of_rule: the top-20 is dominated by the one or two highest-marginal drug pairs (R81 found a median of 2 distinct pairs), and the identity and quality of that best pair do not depend on how many keys the pool holds
honest_note: I went looking for a flaw and did not find one. That matters because R93 and R94 did find flaws; an audit that only ever confirms suspicion would be worth nothing.
limits: uniform subsampling keeps composition fixed, whereas real pools also differ in composition
the 13.17% at the 10k fixed-budget level is noise and must not be read as 'a medium pool is best'
retrospective; no mechanism, clinical or drug-choice claim; no meta-learning or RSI
next_gates: other claims carrying a parenthetical qualifier are candidates for the same audit, one per round, and each must be genuinely able to fail
